"nativeProseFlow": {"paragraphs": [{"index": 0, "blockIndex": 0, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "In real free oscillations, resistance or friction usually causes energy to be dissipated, so the amplitude decreases.
In an ideal model without resistance, free oscillations can continue;"}, {"index": 1, "blockIndex": 0, "paragraphInBlock": 1, "text": "not all free oscillations must quickly die away.
Practical devices often need oscillations that continue."}, {"index": 2, "blockIndex": 0, "paragraphInBlock": 2, "text": "The source calls oscillations whose amplitude does not decrease with time undamped oscillations.
Here we distinguish ideal motion without resistance from motion with resistance that is maintained by energy supplied from outside."}, {"index": 3, "blockIndex": 1, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "Driving a system with a periodic external force is a common way to maintain oscillations.
Whether steady oscillations can develop also depends on the system's response, the driving force, and energy dissipation;
a periodic force alone does not guarantee a constant amplitude."}, {"index": 4, "blockIndex": 2, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "**Oscillations that occur under the action of a periodic external force are called forced oscillations.**
Here, forced means that the motion is driven from outside;
it does not mean that the oscillating object cannot also have its own free oscillations."}, {"index": 5, "blockIndex": 3, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "An external force can transfer energy into a system by doing work on it.
In steady periodic oscillations, the net energy supplied by the driving force over a cycle balances the energy lost through resistance and other causes, so the amplitude no longer gradually decreases."}, {"index": 6, "blockIndex": 3, "paragraphInBlock": 1, "text": "The work done by the external force need not be positive at every instant.
What matters is the net energy balance over the whole cycle.
Continued oscillations do not mean that friction has disappeared or that no external energy source is needed."}, {"index": 7, "blockIndex": 4, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "An object or system that can respond to a periodic external force can undergo forced oscillations, as a periodically driven sieve does in a screening machine.
Its actual response also depends on its supports, constraints, inertia, and energy dissipation;
not every object subjected to any periodic force must oscillate in the same way or with the same amplitude."}, {"index": 8, "blockIndex": 5, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "A system capable of free oscillations is especially worth studying under external driving because it has its own natural frequency.
The source uses a baby in a cradle as an everyday example to illustrate rhythmic pushing.
Here this is a physical analogy for oscillations, not advice about childcare or carrying out the motion."}, {"index": 9, "blockIndex": 6, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "Approximating the cradle as a pendulum gives it a corresponding natural frequency under conditions of small angles and weak resistance.
A constant external force mainly shifts the equilibrium position;"}, {"index": 10, "blockIndex": 6, "paragraphInBlock": 1, "text": "it is not a continuing periodic drive.
The size of this shift depends on the force and the device, so we cannot claim in general that a constant force cannot produce a large displacement."}, {"index": 11, "blockIndex": 6, "paragraphInBlock": 2, "text": "Gentle, irregular pushes in different directions do not readily keep supplying energy to the system in the same rhythm.
Rhythmic pushes that do positive net work on the motion at suitable times may gradually build up noticeable oscillations, even with a small pushing force.
This motion takes time to develop, and the amplitude allowed in practice is still limited by the structure and conditions."}, {"index": 12, "blockIndex": 7, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "The source describes matching the driving rhythm to the rhythm of the cradle's free oscillations as a way to obtain a larger amplitude.
In the approximation of weak resistance and small angles, this matching helps energy to keep entering the system."}, {"index": 13, "blockIndex": 7, "paragraphInBlock": 1, "text": "When the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency, the response may increase greatly.
Equal frequencies alone do not guarantee that any system reaches its maximum amplitude under all conditions.
The response also depends on energy dissipation, the size of the driving force, and the range of motion."}, {"index": 14, "blockIndex": 8, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "When the frequency of a periodic external force is close to an oscillating system's natural frequency, the amplitude of a pendulum or another suitable system may increase greatly.
In the weak-resistance approximation used by the source, this matching is simplified to equal frequencies."}, {"index": 15, "blockIndex": 8, "paragraphInBlock": 1, "text": "The location and size of the maximum response also depend on resistance and the way the system is driven;
an approximate condition is not an exact conclusion for every real system."}, {"index": 16, "blockIndex": 9, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "We now study forced oscillations using a system of springs and a small ball that can undergo free oscillations.
In Figure $17$, the end of a spring is connected to a rope that passes over a pulley, and the rope's other end is connected to an off-center pin on a disk."}, {"index": 17, "blockIndex": 9, "paragraphInBlock": 1, "text": "As a motor turns the disk, the pin moves the rope, periodically driving the spring end and thereby exerting a periodic action on the ball.
The diagram also retains the stands, support rail, the ball's support assembly, and the ruler below.
It is an apparatus schematic, with no precise dimensions or ruler values that can be read from it."}, {"index": 18, "blockIndex": 12, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "Under suitable driving and resistance conditions, the ball starts oscillating from its initial state, and its amplitude can gradually increase.
At first, the motion includes a transient part that depends on the initial conditions."}, {"index": 19, "blockIndex": 12, "paragraphInBlock": 1, "text": "In this stable forced-oscillation model, damping gradually reduces the transient part, and eventually the amplitude no longer changes with time.
The time needed to reach steady motion depends on resistance, driving, and other conditions;"}, {"index": 20, "blockIndex": 12, "paragraphInBlock": 2, "text": "it is not always short.
Under some driving conditions, an undamped system may not have such a finite, steady amplitude, so the source's description cannot be extended to all ideal or real systems."}, {"index": 21, "blockIndex": 13, "paragraphInBlock": 0, "text": "In a linear, stable forced-oscillation model with a single sinusoidal drive, once the transient motion has decayed, the ball's steady-state oscillation frequency equals the driving frequency at the spring end, which is also the frequency of the periodic external force.
